Vice President JD Vance delivered a stunning repudiation of President Trump’s messaging on the Iran War Wednesday morning. He said Republicans lost the midterms because of the war. The 614-word social-media post said many things. But it didn’t say he supported the war. Not once.

   The Iran War and the ensuing rise in gas prices have been the defining issue of Trump’s second term. Vance is seen as a GOP presidential candidate in 2028, and with Trump’s low approval ratings and the Democratic rout in the midterms, Trump’s brand is damaged. 

   So what does Vance do? Stick with the president and possibly lose the MAGA faithful? Or cut himself loose?

   Some Republicans were already looking to take Vance down Wednesday. Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, who is close to the White House, said of Vance: “A good bit of the luster has come off the bloom.”

   Trump’s first Vice President, Mike Pence, didn’t distance himself from Trump until Jan. 6, 2021, the final days of the Trump administration. But Trump saw Pence’s actions that day as such an act of betrayal that Pence’s political career never recovered. In a different way, President Biden’s Vice President, Kamala Harris, had a very difficult time distancing herself from Biden, who had poor approval numbers and struggled to convince Americans that he was in control. Harris was never able to really separate herself from his unpopularity and lost to Trump in 2024.

   So what can Vance do? Can he start carving out a lane for himself now, walking a tightrope that attempts to stay inside Trump’s good graces while also seeming independent? Is that possible with Trump? (Vance recently said if he ran for president, Trump would support him. Trump immediately said this wasn’t true).

   Does Vance support the war in Iran? Does he support Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth? Was this a one-off, or will Vance find new ways to distance himself in the weeks to come? 

   One thing to watch: During the midterm races, Vance got into an extremely tense war of words with Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan. El-Sayed won his race, and now Vance is likely going to be charged with swearing El-Sayed in. Let’s see how both men handle this potentially seismic moment.

   This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       People and Policies I’m Watching   Chuck Schumer : The jubilant Democratic Senate leader made it clear he expects to be re-elected leader of Senate Democrats in the next Congress, but some of his newly elected colleagues aren’t fans.

   Alaska and Mississippi: The two outstanding Senate races are both on a knife-edge.

   Trump appeal: A New York appeals court will hear arguments in Trump’s appeal of his conviction on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to conceal payments to porn actor Stormy Daniels.

   CPAC at Mar-a-Lago: The Conservative Political Action Conference, which has backed Trump and the MAGA movement, hosts its latest gathering in Florida.

   Trump’s Thursday: The president receives an intelligence briefing this morning, then will hold policy meetings throughout the day.

Democrats largely managed to keep the spotlight on the economy as candidates drove home the message that Trump’s policies are hurting pocket books. They kept to this playbook even as a fight for the party’s direction continues to boil.

   America’s AI boom is threatened by an Election Day revolt. Americans’ vote for candidates and ballot measures to ban or slow data center development could rein in AI’s rapid growth and become a big business problem for the companies on the edge of technological progress.    • Israel has ordered billions of dollars’ worth of American military hardware beyond what the U.S. has committed to paying for, showing how hard it would be to phase out Washington’s funding.

   • An appeals court ruled that the rollout of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s new pied-à-terre tax was legal and can move forward.

   • Elon Musk spent $440 million backing Republicans in the midterms and now faces a different reception in Washington when the Democrats take control of Congress.

Vance Breaks With Trump and Steps Into Political Abyss
 
Plus, Democrats’ disciplined messaging on the economy paid off on Election Day, and how midterm results threaten America’s AI boom
 
 
JABIN BOTSFORD FOR WSJ
 

Good morning. Vice President JD Vance delivered a stunning repudiation of President Trump’s messaging on the Iran War Wednesday morning. He said Republicans lost the midterms because of the war. The 614-word social-media post said many things. But it didn’t say he supported the war. Not once.

 

The Iran War and the ensuing rise in gas prices have been the defining issue of Trump’s second term. Vance is seen as a GOP presidential candidate in 2028, and with Trump’s low approval ratings and the Democratic rout in the midterms, Trump’s brand is damaged. 

 

So what does Vance do? Stick with the president and possibly lose the MAGA faithful? Or cut himself loose?

 

Some Republicans were already looking to take Vance down Wednesday. Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, who is close to the White House, said of Vance: “A good bit of the luster has come off the bloom.”

 

Trump’s first Vice President, Mike Pence, didn’t distance himself from Trump until Jan. 6, 2021, the final days of the Trump administration. But Trump saw Pence’s actions that day as such an act of betrayal that Pence’s political career never recovered. In a different way, President Biden’s Vice President, Kamala Harris, had a very difficult time distancing herself from Biden, who had poor approval numbers and struggled to convince Americans that he was in control. Harris was never able to really separate herself from his unpopularity and lost to Trump in 2024.

 

So what can Vance do? Can he start carving out a lane for himself now, walking a tightrope that attempts to stay inside Trump’s good graces while also seeming independent? Is that possible with Trump? (Vance recently said if he ran for president, Trump would support him. Trump immediately said this wasn’t true).

 

Does Vance support the war in Iran? Does he support Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth? Was this a one-off, or will Vance find new ways to distance himself in the weeks to come? 

 

One thing to watch: During the midterm races, Vance got into an extremely tense war of words with Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan. El-Sayed won his race, and now Vance is likely going to be charged with swearing El-Sayed in. Let’s see how both men handle this potentially seismic moment.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Chuck Schumer: The jubilant Democratic Senate leader made it clear he expects to be re-elected leader of Senate Democrats in the next Congress, but some of his newly elected colleagues aren’t fans.

 

Alaska and Mississippi: The two outstanding Senate races are both on a knife-edge.

 

Trump appeal: A New York appeals court will hear arguments in Trump’s appeal of his conviction on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to conceal payments to porn actor Stormy Daniels.

 

CPAC at Mar-a-Lago: The Conservative Political Action Conference, which has backed Trump and the MAGA movement, hosts its latest gathering in Florida.

 

Trump’s Thursday: The president receives an intelligence briefing this morning, then will hold policy meetings throughout the day.

What I’m Following

 
 
ROBIN RAYNE/ZUMA PRESS
 

Democrats focused on the economy to secure the party’s historic victory. Democrats largely managed to keep the spotlight on the economy as candidates drove home the message that Trump’s policies are hurting pocket books. They kept to this playbook even as a fight for the party’s direction continues to boil.

 

America’s AI boom is threatened by an Election Day revolt. Americans’ vote for candidates and ballot measures to ban or slow data center development could rein in AI’s rapid growth and become a big business problem for the companies on the edge of technological progress. It also threatens to hobble a boom powering the U.S. economy.

 

After two years of unchecked power, Trump is facing a new reality. In the span of just a few hours on Tuesday, the power dynamic for the remaining two years of the Trump presidency shifted dramatically. If Trump wants to accomplish anything durable going forward, he will have to accept limits to his authority and compromise—things he’s shown little interest in doing during his political career.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• The U.S. was unprepared for drone warfare, the Pentagon’s technology chief said at the WSJ Tech conference.

 

• Israel has ordered billions of dollars’ worth of American military hardware beyond what the U.S. has committed to paying for, showing how hard it would be to phase out Washington’s funding.

 

• An appeals court ruled that the rollout of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s new pied-à-terre tax was legal and can move forward.

 

• Elon Musk spent $440 million backing Republicans in the midterms and now faces a different reception in Washington when the Democrats take control of Congress.

I’m Damian Paletta, The Wall Street Journal’s Washington coverage chief. I’ve covered Washington for 22 years as a reporter and editor. I’ve covered the White House, Congress, national security, the federal budget, economics and multiple market meltdowns.
